title: Lab 1 review: nerves, reflexes and general senses
summary: Resting and action potentials, summation, the reflex arc and the reflexes you test, and the receptors of the skin.
objectives: Explain why the resting potential is negative and what changes it
Distinguish graded potentials from action potentials and temporal from spatial summation
Name the five parts of a reflex arc and the nerve and segments of each stretch reflex
Match each skin receptor to what it senses and explain referred pain
takeaways: Resting potential ≈ −70 mV, set mainly by K+; the Na+/K+ pump keeps the gradients.
An axon's spike is all-or-none; a nerve's compound action potential is graded by recruitment.
Receptor → sensory neuron → integration centre → motor neuron → effector.
Patellar L2–L4 femoral; biceps C5–C6; triceps C6–C8; calcaneal S1–S2.
Meissner: light touch. Pacinian: pressure and vibration. Free endings: pain and temperature.

steps.title: The resting potential
steps.text: A neuron has dendrites, a cell body and an axon; a nerve is a cable of many axons wrapped in endoneurium, perineurium and epineurium. At rest the inside of the cell is about −70 mV. That voltage is set mainly by K+ leaking out through open channels, so raising extracellular K+ depolarises the cell. Changing extracellular Na+ does little at rest, because few Na+ channels are open. The Na+/K+ pump, which ouabain blocks, keeps the gradients.

check.q: What happens to the resting potential when extracellular K+ is raised, and why?
check.a: It becomes less negative (depolarises), because a smaller K+ gradient drives less K+ out.

steps.title: Graded potentials and summation
steps.text:
At a synapse an EPSP is a small depolarisation and an IPSP a small hyperpolarisation. Both are graded and fade with time and distance, but they add. Temporal summation is one input firing again before its first potential has faded; spatial summation is several inputs firing together. An EPSP and an IPSP arriving together can cancel. If the sum reaches threshold at the axon hillock, an action potential fires.

On the neuron model, find the axon hillock.

check.q: What is the difference between temporal and spatial summation?
check.a: Temporal: one synapse fires repeatedly in quick succession. Spatial: several synapses fire at the same time.

steps.title: Action potentials and whole nerves
steps.text: An axon's action potential is all-or-none: voltage-gated Na+ channels open to depolarise, K+ channels to repolarise. In the absolute refractory period no second spike is possible; in the relative one a stronger stimulus is needed. A whole nerve gives a compound action potential that grows from threshold to maximal stimulus as more axons are recruited. Thick myelinated A fibres conduct fastest, thin unmyelinated C fibres slowest; local anaesthetics and cold block conduction.

check.q: Why is a nerve's compound action potential graded when each axon's spike is all-or-none?
check.a: Stronger stimuli recruit more axons (with higher thresholds), so more spikes add together.

steps.title: The reflex arc
steps.text: A reflex is a fast, involuntary, predictable response. It has five parts: receptor → sensory (afferent) neuron → integration centre → motor (efferent) neuron → effector. The sensory cell body sits in the dorsal root ganglion and its axon enters by the dorsal root; the motor axon leaves by the ventral root. Somatic reflexes move skeletal muscle; visceral reflexes act on smooth muscle, heart or glands. A stretch reflex is monosynaptic; most others are polysynaptic.

check.q: List the five parts of a reflex arc in order.
check.a: Receptor, sensory neuron, integration centre, motor neuron, effector.

steps.title: The reflexes you test
steps.text: Stretch reflexes start in the muscle spindle. Patellar: the knee extends (femoral nerve, L2–L4). Biceps: the elbow flexes (musculocutaneous, C5–C6). Triceps: the elbow extends (radial, C6–C8). Calcaneal: the foot plantar flexes (tibial, S1–S2). The corneal reflex runs in on the trigeminal nerve and out on the facial. Stroking the sole normally curls the toes; a Babinski sign (big toe up, toes fan) is normal in infants but means corticospinal damage in adults.

check.q: Which nerve and spinal segments serve the patellar reflex?
check.a: The femoral nerve, L2–L4.

steps.title: Skin receptors and referred pain
steps.text: Meissner corpuscles in the dermal papillae sense light touch and adapt fast; Merkel discs sense light touch and adapt slowly; deep Pacinian corpuscles sense pressure and vibration; free nerve endings sense pain and temperature. Two-point discrimination is finest on the fingertips, where receptors are densest. Referred pain is visceral pain felt on skin served by the same spinal segments: heart to the left chest and arm, gallbladder to the right shoulder, appendix first around the umbilicus.
focus: Distal phalanx of second finger of hand

check.q: Which skin receptor senses vibration, and where is it?
check.a: The Pacinian (lamellated) corpuscle, deep in the dermis and hypodermis.

practice.q: Put the reflex arc in order
During the absolute refractory period:
choices: A stronger than normal stimulus is needed
The Na+/K+ pump is switched off
No stimulus, however strong, can fire a second action potential
practice.why: The Na+ channels are inactivated; in the relative refractory period a stronger stimulus works.

practice.q: A Babinski sign in an adult points to damage of the:
practice.why: It is normal in infants, whose corticospinal tracts are not yet fully myelinated.

title: Lab 2 review: the eye and vision
summary: Accessory structures, the six eye muscles, the tunics and chambers, the retina and the visual pathway.
objectives: Trace tears from the lacrimal gland to the nose
Name the six extrinsic eye muscles and their nerves
Identify the three tunics, the chambers and the humors of the eyeball
Explain accommodation, the fovea and the blind spot, and trace the visual pathway
takeaways: Lacrimal gland → puncta → canaliculi → lacrimal sac → nasolacrimal duct → nose.
LR6 SO4, the rest 3.
Fibrous (sclera, cornea), vascular (choroid, ciliary body, iris), sensory (retina).
Near vision: ciliary muscle contracts, zonules slacken, lens rounds up.
Nasal fibres cross at the chiasm; the visual cortex is in the occipital lobe.

steps.title: Accessory structures and tears
steps.text: The conjunctiva lines the lids (palpebral) and covers the white of the eye (bulbar); tarsal glands oil the lid margin. Tears come from the lacrimal gland in the upper lateral orbit, wash across the eye, and drain through the lacrimal puncta → canaliculi → lacrimal sac → nasolacrimal duct into the nasal cavity, which is why crying makes your nose run. Tears contain lysozyme, an antibacterial enzyme.

check.q: Trace a tear from where it is made to where it drains.
check.a: Lacrimal gland → across the eye → lacrimal puncta → canaliculi → lacrimal sac → nasolacrimal duct → nasal cavity.

steps.title: Six muscles, three nerves
steps.text: Four recti (superior, inferior, medial, lateral) and two obliques move the eye. The superior oblique runs through the trochlea and turns the eye down and out; the inferior oblique turns it up and out. Nerves: LR6 SO4, the rest 3. The lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens (VI), the superior oblique by the trochlear (IV), and every other eye muscle, plus levator palpebrae superioris, by the oculomotor nerve (III).

check.q: Which nerve supplies the lateral rectus, and which the superior oblique?
check.a: Lateral rectus: abducens (VI). Superior oblique: trochlear (IV).

steps.title: Three tunics, two segments
steps.text: Fibrous tunic: the white sclera and the clear cornea. Vascular tunic: the choroid, the ciliary body (whose muscle focuses the lens) and the iris, whose sphincter pupillae narrows the pupil and dilator pupillae widens it. Sensory tunic: the retina. In front of the lens, aqueous humor is made by the ciliary processes and drains into the scleral venous sinus; behind it, the gel-like vitreous humor holds the retina in place.

check.q: Where is aqueous humor made, and where does it drain?
check.a: Made by the ciliary processes; drains through the scleral venous sinus (canal of Schlemm).

steps.title: Retina and focusing
steps.text: Light passes the ganglion and bipolar cells to reach the rods (dim light, no colour) and cones (bright light, colour, detail). The fovea centralis, in the macula, is all cones and gives the sharpest vision; the optic disc, where the nerve leaves, has no receptors and is the blind spot. For near vision the ciliary muscle contracts, the zonular fibres slacken and the lens rounds up. Myopia focuses in front of the retina (concave lens), hyperopia behind it (convex lens).

check.q: What does the ciliary muscle do when you focus on something close?
check.a: It contracts, slackening the zonular fibres so the elastic lens becomes rounder.

steps.title: The visual pathway and pupils
steps.text: Retina → optic nerve → optic chiasm, where fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross → optic tract → lateral geniculate body of the thalamus → optic radiation → visual cortex in the occipital lobe. So each side of the brain sees the opposite half of the visual field. Some fibres go to the superior colliculi for visual reflexes. Light in one eye constricts both pupils: the direct and the consensual response. The efferent limb is the oculomotor nerve.

check.q: Which retinal fibres cross at the optic chiasm?
check.a: Those from the medial (nasal) half of each retina.

practice.q: Put the visual pathway in order
A myopic (near-sighted) eye is corrected with a:
practice.why: Myopia focuses in front of the retina; a diverging lens pushes the focus back.

practice.q: The commonest colour blindness is:
choices: Red–green, inherited on the X chromosome
practice.why: A missing or faulty red or green cone pigment; it is X-linked, so far commoner in males.

title: Lab 2 review: the ear, hearing and balance
summary: Outer, middle and inner ear, how the cochlea turns sound into signals, hearing tests, and the organs of balance.
objectives: Identify the parts of the external and middle ear and the three ossicles
Describe the scalae, fluids and spiral organ of the cochlea
Tell conduction from sensorineural deafness with the Weber and Rinne tests
Contrast the maculae (static balance) with the cristae (dynamic balance)
takeaways: Malleus → incus → stapes → oval window.
Perilymph in the scala vestibuli and tympani; endolymph in the cochlear duct.
Weber lateralises to a conduction-deaf ear; Rinne shows bone louder than air in conduction deafness.
Maculae (utricle, saccule): head position. Cristae (ampullae): rotation.

steps.title: Outer and middle ear
steps.text: The external ear is the auricle, built on elastic cartilage, and the external acoustic meatus, which ends at the tympanic membrane. The air-filled middle ear holds the ossicles malleus → incus → stapes; the stapes footplate sits in the oval window, and funnelling sound onto that small window amplifies it. The tensor tympani and stapedius damp loud sounds. The auditory tube joins the middle ear to the nasopharynx and equalises pressure.

check.q: Name the ossicles in order from the eardrum.
check.a: Malleus, incus, stapes.

steps.title: The cochlea
steps.text: The inner ear is a bony labyrinth of perilymph around a membranous labyrinth of endolymph. The cochlea coils three channels: the scala vestibuli (from the oval window), the cochlear duct and the scala tympani (ending at the round window). On the basilar membrane sits the spiral organ (of Corti): hair cells whose stereocilia bend against the tectorial membrane. High pitches peak near the base of the cochlea, low pitches near its apex.

check.q: Which fluid fills the cochlear duct, and which fills the scala tympani?
check.a: Endolymph in the cochlear duct; perilymph in the scala tympani (and scala vestibuli).

steps.title: Hearing pathway and hearing tests
steps.text: Cochlear nerve → cochlear nuclei → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate body → auditory cortex in the temporal lobe. Conduction deafness is a block in the outer or middle ear (wax, a torn drum, stiff ossicles); sensorineural deafness is hair-cell or nerve damage. Weber: a fork on the forehead sounds louder in a conduction-deaf ear, softer in a nerve-deaf one. Rinne: air conduction normally outlasts bone; with conduction deafness bone is heard longer.

check.q: With conduction deafness in the left ear, where is the Weber tone heard?
check.a: Louder in the left (affected) ear.

steps.title: Static balance: utricle and saccule
steps.text: The vestibule holds two sacs, the utricle and saccule. Each has a macula: hair cells whose stereocilia poke into a gel otolithic membrane weighted with calcium carbonate crystals, the otoliths. When the head tilts or moves in a straight line, the heavy membrane slides and bends the hair cells. This is static equilibrium: the sense of head position relative to gravity.

check.q: What bends the hair cells of a macula when you tilt your head?
check.a: The otolithic membrane, weighted with otoliths, slides with gravity.

steps.title: Dynamic balance: semicircular canals
steps.text: Three semicircular canals lie at right angles, one for each plane. Each swells into an ampulla holding a crista ampullaris, whose hair cells are capped by a gel cupula. When the head turns, the endolymph lags and bends the cupula: dynamic equilibrium, the sense of rotation. After spinning stops the fluid keeps moving, giving vertigo and nystagmus. The Romberg test (standing still, eyes closed) checks that vestibular and proprioceptive input can hold you up without vision.

check.q: What detects rotation of the head, and how?
check.a: The cristae ampullares of the semicircular canals: lagging endolymph bends the cupula and its hair cells.

practice.q: Put the path of sound in order
In the Rinne test, bone conduction is heard longer than air conduction. This means:
practice.why: Normally air conduction outlasts bone; a middle- or outer-ear block reverses it.

title: Lab 3 review: blood
summary: Plasma and formed elements, the five white cells and how to recognise them, and the differential count.
objectives: State what plasma contains and describe erythrocytes and platelets
Identify the five leukocytes on a smear and give their normal percentages and roles
Rank the leukocytes in a normal differential count and interpret a shift
takeaways: Plasma ≈ 55% of blood, ≈ 91% water; albumin is the main protein.
RBCs: anucleate biconcave discs, ≈ 5 million/mm³, live ≈ 120 days.
Neutrophils > lymphocytes > monocytes > eosinophils > basophils.
Neutrophils: bacteria. Eosinophils: allergy and parasites. Basophils: histamine and heparin.

steps.title: Plasma, red cells and platelets
steps.text: Blood is about 55% plasma, which is about 91% water carrying proteins (albumin, globulins, fibrinogen, mostly made by the liver), ions, nutrients, hormones and wastes, and 45% formed elements. Erythrocytes are the most numerous cell, about 5 million per mm³: pink, anucleate, biconcave discs about 7.5 µm across that live about 120 days. Platelets (250,000–400,000/mm³) are purple fragments of megakaryocytes that start clotting. All are made in red bone marrow.

check.q: Why is an erythrocyte biconcave?
check.a: It gives a large surface area for its volume, speeding gas exchange, and lets it bend through capillaries.

steps.title: The granulocytes
steps.text: White cells (about 5,000–9,000/mm³) squeeze out of capillaries by diapedesis. Neutrophils (60–70%) have a nucleus of 2–5 lobes and pale granules; they eat bacteria and rise in acute bacterial infection. Eosinophils (2–4%) have a two-lobed nucleus and red-orange granules; they rise in allergy and parasitic worm infection. Basophils (under 1%) have dark blue-purple granules that hide the nucleus; the granules hold histamine and heparin.

check.q: How do you tell an eosinophil from a basophil on a stained smear?
check.a: Eosinophil: bilobed nucleus with red-orange granules. Basophil: dark purple granules that hide the nucleus.

steps.title: Lymphocytes and monocytes
steps.text: Lymphocytes (20–25%) have a large round nucleus with a thin rim of blue cytoplasm. B cells become plasma cells that make antibodies (humoral immunity); T cells mature in the thymus and attack infected or abnormal cells directly (cell-mediated immunity). Monocytes (3–8%) are the largest white cells, with a kidney- or U-shaped nucleus; in the tissues they become macrophages, and their number rises in chronic infection.

check.q: Where do T cells mature, and what kind of immunity do they give?
check.a: In the thymus; cell-mediated immunity.

steps.title: The differential count
steps.text: A differential count classifies 100 white cells on a stained smear and reports each type as a percentage. The normal order, commonest first, is neutrophils > lymphocytes > monocytes > eosinophils > basophils: Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas. A shift is a clue: neutrophils climb in acute bacterial infection such as appendicitis, eosinophils in allergy or parasites, lymphocytes in many viral infections.

check.q: Give the normal ranking of white cells, commonest first.
check.a: Neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils.

practice.q: Rank the white cells, commonest first
Histamine and heparin are stored in the granules of:
practice.why: Histamine dilates vessels; heparin stops clotting.

practice.q: A differential count shows 12% eosinophils. The likeliest cause is:
choices: A parasitic worm infection or allergy
practice.why: Normal is 2–4%; allergy and parasites raise eosinophils.

practice.q: Give the normal red cell count, diameter and lifespan.
practice.a: About 5 million per mm³, about 7.5 µm across, about 120 days.

title: Lab 3 review: the heart
summary: Where the heart sits, its coverings and wall, blood flow through the chambers, the valves, the coronary vessels and the sheep heart.
objectives: Describe the heart's position, the pericardium and the three layers of its wall
Trace blood through the four chambers and valves
Identify the valves, chordae, papillary muscles and interior features
Name the main coronary arteries and cardiac veins and orient a sheep heart
takeaways: Apex at the 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line; base at the 2nd.
RA → tricuspid → RV → pulmonary valve → lungs → LA → mitral → LV → aortic valve.
Chordae and papillary muscles stop AV cusps everting.
LCA → LAD + circumflex; RCA → posterior interventricular. Veins → coronary sinus → RA.

steps.title: Position, pericardium and wall
steps.text: The heart lies in the mediastinum, behind the sternum and on the diaphragm, tipped to the left. Its base, with the great vessels, is at the 2nd intercostal space; its apex points to the 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line. It sits in the tough fibrous pericardium, lined by the parietal serous layer; the visceral layer is the epicardium, with fluid between them. The wall: epicardium, thick myocardium, and endocardium.

check.q: Name the layers from the outside of the pericardium to the heart's lumen.
check.a: Fibrous pericardium, parietal serous pericardium, pericardial cavity, epicardium (visceral pericardium), myocardium, endocardium.

steps.micro_view: Pericardium: The heart in its pericardium

steps.title: Blood through the heart
steps.text: Venae cavae and coronary sinus → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary trunk → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta. Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood and pulmonary veins oxygenated blood: arteries leave the heart, whatever they carry. The left ventricle's wall is much thicker, because it pumps into the high-pressure systemic circuit.

check.q: Why is the left ventricle's wall thicker than the right's?
check.a: It pumps blood around the whole body against much higher (systemic) pressure.

steps.title: Valves and the inside of the heart
steps.text: The atrioventricular valves, tricuspid on the right and mitral (bicuspid) on the left, are tied by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles, which stop the cusps everting as the ventricles contract. The pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves, three cusps each, stop blood falling back as the ventricles relax. Inside: pectinate muscles in the atria, trabeculae carneae in the ventricles, and the fossa ovalis, remnant of the fetal foramen ovale.

check.q: What do the chordae tendineae and papillary muscles do?
check.a: They hold the AV valve cusps so they cannot evert into the atria when the ventricles contract.

steps.title: Coronary vessels
steps.text: The left and right coronary arteries leave the ascending aorta just above the aortic valve. The left divides into the anterior interventricular artery in the anterior interventricular sulcus and the circumflex in the coronary sulcus. The right runs in the coronary sulcus and gives the right marginal and the posterior interventricular artery. The great, middle and small cardiac veins drain into the coronary sinus, which opens into the right atrium. The coronaries fill mainly in diastole.

check.q: Name the two branches of the left coronary artery.
check.a: The anterior interventricular artery and the circumflex artery.

steps.title: The sheep heart
steps.text: The sheep heart has the human plan, but its venae cavae are called anterior and posterior, and it carries more epicardial fat. To orient it, find the pulmonary trunk in front, leaving the right ventricle, with the aorta right behind it, leaving the left. The left ventricle feels firm and thick-walled; the right is thinner and softer. Pulmonary veins open into the left atrium, and the coronary sinus into the back of the right atrium.

check.q: How can you tell the ventricles apart on an intact sheep heart?
check.a: The left ventricle is firm and thick-walled; the right is thinner and softer. The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle at the front.

practice.q: Put blood flow through the heart in order
Which vessels carry oxygen-rich blood into the heart?
practice.why: They return blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

practice.micro_view: Pericardium: The heart in its pericardium

title: Lab 4 review: the ECG and heart function
summary: The conduction system, what each ECG wave means and how to read the paper, common abnormalities, the axis, heart sounds and rate control.
objectives: Trace the impulse through the conduction system
Name the ECG waves and intervals, give normal values and calculate heart rate
Recognise blocks and arrhythmias and explain axis deviation
Link heart sounds to valve closure and name the auscultation sites
takeaways: SA node → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres.
P = atrial depolarisation; QRS = ventricular depolarisation; T = ventricular repolarisation.
Small square 0.04 s; heart rate = 60 ÷ R–R (s).
PR > 0.20 s = first-degree block; QRS > 0.12 s = bundle branch block.
S1 = AV valves close; S2 = semilunar valves close.

steps.title: The conduction system
steps.text: The SA node in the wall of the right atrium is the pacemaker, about 70–80 beats a minute: its cells never rest but drift up to threshold (the pacemaker potential). The impulse spreads over the atria to the AV node, which delays it so the atria can empty, then down the AV bundle (of His), the right and left bundle branches in the septum and the Purkinje fibres. Contractile cells have a long plateau, so their long refractory period prevents tetanus.

check.q: Why does the AV node delay the impulse?
check.a: So the atria finish contracting and emptying into the ventricles before the ventricles contract.

steps.micro_view: Conduction: Whole pathway, right heart opened

steps.title: Waves, intervals and the paper
steps.text: P wave = atrial depolarisation; QRS = ventricular depolarisation (atrial repolarisation hides in it); T wave = ventricular repolarisation. The PR interval (0.12–0.20 s) includes the AV-node delay; QRS lasts 0.08–0.10 s; QT about 0.36 s. At 25 mm/s a small square is 0.04 s and a large one 0.20 s, and heart rate = 60 ÷ R–R interval in seconds. Lead II (right arm negative, left leg positive) usually gives the clearest trace.

check.q: The R–R interval is 20 small squares. What is the heart rate?
check.a: 20 × 0.04 = 0.8 s; 60 ÷ 0.8 = 75 beats per minute.

steps.title: Rates, blocks and arrhythmias
steps.text: Tachycardia is a resting rate over 100 a minute; bradycardia under 60, normal in trained athletes. A first-degree block stretches PR beyond 0.20 s; in complete block P waves and QRS complexes run independently, the ventricles at 30–40 a minute. Bundle branch block widens QRS beyond 0.12 s. A PVC is an early, wide QRS with no P wave; atrial fibrillation has no clear P waves and an irregular rhythm. Exercise shortens R–R, mostly the T–P segment.

check.q: What ECG sign defines a first-degree heart block?
check.a: A PR interval longer than 0.20 s.

steps.title: The mean electrical axis
steps.text: The mean electrical axis is the average direction of ventricular depolarisation, running roughly along the interventricular septum, down and to the left. It is found by plotting the net QRS deflections of leads I and III on a circle; normal is about 0° to +90°. Left axis deviation suggests left ventricular hypertrophy or left bundle branch block; right axis deviation suggests right ventricular hypertrophy. The three limb leads form Einthoven's triangle; the right leg electrode is the ground.

check.q: What does right axis deviation suggest?
check.a: Right ventricular hypertrophy (or the heart displaced to the right).

steps.title: Heart sounds, pulse and rate control
steps.text: S1 (lubb) is the AV valves closing as systole starts; S2 (dupp) is the semilunar valves closing as diastole starts. A murmur is turbulent flow through a leaky or narrowed valve. Listen for the aortic valve at the right 2nd intercostal space, pulmonary at the left 2nd, tricuspid at the lower left sternal border, and mitral at the apex. Count the pulse at the radial or carotid artery. Sympathetic nerves speed the heart; the vagus slows it.

check.q: What causes the first and the second heart sound?
check.a: S1: closure of the AV (tricuspid and mitral) valves. S2: closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves.

practice.q: Put the conduction system in order
The T wave shows:
practice.why: Atrial repolarisation is hidden in the QRS.

practice.q: A QRS lasting 0.14 s suggests:
practice.why: Normal QRS is 0.08–0.10 s; over 0.12 s means the ventricles depolarise out of step.

practice.q: Warming a frog heart from room temperature to 37 °C:
practice.why: Ion channels and enzymes work faster when warm; cold slows the rate.

title: Lab 5 review: vessel walls and the arteries
summary: The three tunics, and the arterial tree from the aortic arch to the brain, the limbs and the abdomen.
objectives: Name the three tunics and tell an artery from a vein on a slide
Name the branches of the aortic arch and of the carotid arteries
Describe the cerebral arterial circle
Trace the arteries of the upper and lower limbs and list the branches of the abdominal aorta
takeaways: Intima, media, externa; arteries thick media, veins thin media with valves.
Arch: brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian.
Subclavian → axillary → brachial → radial and ulnar.
External iliac → femoral → popliteal → anterior and posterior tibial.
Coeliac trunk: left gastric, splenic, common hepatic.

steps.title: Vessel walls
steps.text: Every vessel larger than a capillary has three tunics: the tunica intima (endothelium on thin connective tissue), the tunica media (smooth muscle and elastic fibres) and the tunica externa (collagen, carrying the vessel's own vasa vasorum and nerves). Arteries have a thick media and a round lumen; elastic arteries like the aorta are packed with elastic sheets, while muscular arteries have internal and external elastic laminae. Veins have a thin media, a wide lumen and valves.

check.q: How do you tell an artery from its companion vein on a slide?
check.a: The artery has a thicker media and a round, open lumen; the vein has a thin wall, a wide often collapsed lumen, and may show valves.

steps.title: The arch and the head
steps.text: The aortic arch has three branches, right to left: the brachiocephalic trunk (splitting into the right subclavian and right common carotid), the left common carotid and the left subclavian. Each common carotid forks at the level of the upper thyroid cartilage into the internal carotid (to the brain; its swollen start is the carotid sinus) and the external carotid (face and scalp). The vertebral arteries climb through the cervical vertebrae and join as the basilar artery.

check.q: Name the three branches of the aortic arch, from right to left.
check.a: Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, left subclavian artery.

steps.title: The circle of Willis
steps.text: Four arteries feed the brain: two internal carotids and two vertebrals. Beneath the brain they link into the cerebral arterial circle: the anterior cerebral arteries joined by the anterior communicating artery, the internal carotids, the posterior communicating arteries, and the posterior cerebral arteries from the basilar. The middle cerebral artery continues the internal carotid. If one feeding artery narrows, the circle can still carry blood to the whole brain.

check.q: Which arteries join the carotid and vertebral systems in the circle?
check.a: The posterior communicating arteries.

steps.title: Limb arteries
steps.text: Upper limb: subclavian → axillary (after the first rib) → brachial (the blood pressure artery) → at the elbow radial and ulnar → the superficial and deep palmar arches. Lower limb: common iliac → external iliac → femoral (under the inguinal ligament; gives the deep femoral) → popliteal behind the knee → anterior tibial, which becomes the dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial, which gives the fibular artery. The internal iliac feeds the pelvis.

check.q: Which artery becomes the dorsalis pedis?
check.a: The anterior tibial artery.

steps.title: The abdominal aorta
steps.text: Below the diaphragm the aorta gives, top to bottom: the inferior phrenic arteries; the coeliac trunk (left gastric, splenic and common hepatic, for the stomach, spleen and liver); the superior mesenteric (small intestine, right colon and most of the transverse colon); the paired suprarenal, renal and gonadal arteries; the inferior mesenteric (left colon and upper rectum); lumbar arteries; and the median sacral. At L4 it splits into the common iliac arteries.

check.q: Name the three branches of the coeliac trunk.
check.a: Left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries.

practice.q: Trace blood from the aorta to the left hand
Trace blood from the aorta to the top of the foot

title: Lab 5 review: veins, the portal system and fetal circulation
summary: Venous sinuses and neck veins, limb veins, the venae cavae and azygos, the hepatic portal system and the fetal shunts.
objectives: Trace venous blood from the brain to the superior vena cava
Identify the superficial veins of the arm and leg
Name the tributaries of the inferior vena cava and the azygos system
Describe the hepatic portal system and the three fetal shunts and their remnants
takeaways: Dural sinuses → internal jugular → brachiocephalic → superior vena cava.
Cephalic, basilic, median cubital; great and small saphenous.
The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein.
Splenic + superior mesenteric → hepatic portal vein → liver sinusoids → hepatic veins → IVC.
Foramen ovale → fossa ovalis; ductus arteriosus → ligamentum arteriosum; ductus venosus → ligamentum venosum.

steps.title: Veins of the head and neck
steps.text: The brain drains into the dural venous sinuses: superior and inferior sagittal, straight, transverse and sigmoid, which leaves the skull as the internal jugular vein. The cavernous sinus beside the pituitary receives the ophthalmic veins. The internal jugular joins the subclavian to form the brachiocephalic vein, and the two brachiocephalics make the superior vena cava. The superficial external jugular drains the scalp and face into the subclavian.

check.q: Which sinus becomes the internal jugular vein?
check.a: The sigmoid sinus.

steps.title: Limb veins
steps.text: Deep veins travel with the arteries and share their names; superficial veins run alone under the skin. In the arm the cephalic (lateral) and basilic (medial) veins are joined at the elbow by the median cubital vein, the usual site for drawing blood. In the leg the great saphenous vein, the longest in the body, climbs the medial side from the dorsal venous arch to the femoral vein; the small saphenous climbs the back of the calf to the popliteal vein.

check.q: Which vein is usually used to draw blood, and which two veins does it join?
check.a: The median cubital vein, linking the cephalic and basilic veins.

steps.title: Venae cavae and azygos
steps.text: The inferior vena cava collects the common iliac, lumbar, renal, right gonadal and hepatic veins; the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein instead. The azygos system drains the back of the chest wall: the azygos on the right, and the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos on the left, which cross to it; the azygos then arches into the superior vena cava. Everything ends in the right atrium, via the SVC, the IVC and the coronary sinus.

check.q: Where does the left testicular (or ovarian) vein drain?
check.a: Into the left renal vein.

steps.title: The hepatic portal system
steps.text: Blood from the stomach, intestines, spleen and pancreas does not go straight to the IVC. The splenic vein, joined by the inferior mesenteric, meets the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein. It carries nutrient-rich blood into the liver sinusoids, a second capillary bed, where it is processed and cleaned; it leaves by the hepatic veins into the IVC.

check.q: Which two veins join to form the hepatic portal vein?
check.a: The splenic vein and the superior mesenteric vein.

steps.title: Fetal circulation
steps.text: The placenta does the fetus's breathing. The umbilical vein brings oxygenated blood; much of it bypasses the liver through the ductus venosus into the IVC. In the heart blood skips the lungs twice: right to left atrium through the foramen ovale, and pulmonary trunk to aorta through the ductus arteriosus. Two umbilical arteries, from the internal iliacs, take blood back. After birth they close into the fossa ovalis, ligamentum arteriosum, ligamentum venosum and round ligament of the liver.

check.q: What does the ductus arteriosus become after birth?
check.a: The ligamentum arteriosum.

practice.q: Trace blood from the small intestine back to the heart
Which fetal vessel carries the most oxygen-rich blood?
practice.why: It brings blood straight from the placenta.

Light entering the eye: put what it passes in order
The patellar reflex: put the events in order
items: Sensory neuron in the femoral nerve

practice.q: One heartbeat: put the events in order
Why does a cardiac contractile cell have a plateau in its action potential, unlike an axon?
choices: Slow Ca2+ entry holds it depolarised
practice.why: The Ca2+ plateau lengthens the refractory period so the heart cannot be tetanised.

practice.q: Cooling slows which of these?
choices: Both nerve conduction and heart rate
practice.why: Ion channels open and close more slowly when cold.

practice.q: Which pair are both parasympathetic effects?
choices: Pupil dilation and slowing of the heart
Pupil constriction and faster heart rate
Pupil constriction and slowing of the heart
Pupil dilation and faster heart rate
practice.why: The oculomotor nerve constricts the pupil; the vagus slows the SA node.

practice.q: Hair cells with stereocilia are the receptors for:
choices: Hearing, head position and head rotation
practice.why: Spiral organ, maculae and cristae all use hair cells; only the overlying membrane differs.

practice.q: The endocardium is continuous with which layer of the blood vessels?
choices: The endothelium of the tunica intima
practice.why: One continuous endothelium lines the heart and every vessel.

practice.q: Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood?
practice.why: Arteries and veins are named by direction, not oxygen: the pulmonary trunk and umbilical arteries carry the poorest blood.

practice.q: An adult with appendicitis has a raised white count. Which cell has risen, and where is the early pain felt?
practice.why: Acute bacterial infection raises neutrophils; early appendix pain is referred to the periumbilical region.

practice.q: The mean electrical axis normally runs roughly parallel to the:
practice.why: Ventricular depolarisation spreads down the septum toward the apex, down and to the left.

practice.q: Which receptor starts the patellar reflex, and which senses head rotation?
practice.why: Spindles sense stretch; the cristae in the semicircular canals sense rotation.

practice.q: Which two arteries are the usual sites for counting a pulse?
practice.why: Both lie near the surface over something firm.

practice.q: Name the cranial nerve for each: lateral rectus, sensation from the cornea, closing the eye in the corneal reflex, constricting the pupil, slowing the heart.
practice.a: Abducens (VI); trigeminal, ophthalmic division (V1); facial (VII); oculomotor (III); vagus (X).

practice.q: Which fetal structures leave remnants you can find on an adult heart, and what are they called?
practice.a: The foramen ovale leaves the fossa ovalis; the ductus arteriosus leaves the ligamentum arteriosum.

practice.q: What makes the hepatic portal system different from ordinary venous drainage?
practice.a: Blood passes through two capillary beds in a row: gut and spleen capillaries drain via the hepatic portal vein into the liver sinusoids before returning to the heart through the hepatic veins.

practice.q: Why do both the lens and a heart valve need tethers, and what are they called?
practice.a: The lens is held by zonular fibres (suspensory ligament) pulled by the ciliary body; AV valve cusps are held by chordae tendineae pulled by papillary muscles.
